Looking at nginx Ingress, here is the information gather by my 'agent'... Short answer: the controller does not special‐case, normalize, or reject IP addresses in the Ingress rule hosts. It passes the string through and renders it into NGINX’s server_name as-is. That has different outcomes for IPv4 vs IPv6. What happens in code - Host is taken verbatim into the Server object - controller.createServers(): rule.Host is copied into server.Hostname (empty -> "_") with no IP/DNS validation - file: internal/ingress/controller/controller.go - The NGINX template renders server_name using that hostname unchanged (except for wildcard handling) - template: server_name {{ buildServerName $server.Hostname }} ... - file: rootfs/etc/nginx/template/nginx.tmpl - buildServerName only rewrites wildcard names; otherwise returns the input string - file: internal/ingress/controller/template/template.go (buildServerName) - Admission/safety checks do not reject IP hosts - inspector.CheckRegex() only blocks dangerous substrings (alias/root/etc); it does not validate DNS vs IP - file: internal/ingress/inspector/{ingress.go,rules.go} - TLS certificate selection for such a host will use the host string - verifyHostname() treats IPs specially and only matches against IP SANs - file: internal/ingress/controller/certificate.go (verifyHostname) Resulting behavior - IPv4 host (e.g., 203.0.113.10) - NGINX gets: server_name 203.0.113.10; This is valid in NGINX and will match requests whose Host header is that IP. - TLS: the controller will associate a cert only if it has the IP in its SANs; otherwise it falls back to the default cert. Note many clients don’t send SNI for IP literals, so the default cert may be served at handshake time regardless. - IPv6 host (e.g., 2001:db8::1) - NGINX would be rendered with: server_name 2001:db8::1; Colons aren’t valid in server_name tokens. On reload, the controller runs nginx -t (testTemplate in internal/ingress/controller/nginx.go); nginx -t will fail, so the reload is aborted and the previous (last good) config stays active. Bottom line - The controller accepts and forwards IP hosts unchanged. - IPv4 literal hosts work (host-based vhost keyed to the IP in the Host header); TLS requires an IP SAN to avoid cert mismatch. - IPv6 literal hosts cause an invalid NGINX configuration and prevent reload. /inline_code

There are multiple issues here, lets split them: 1) On gang scheduling semantics for LWS vs Deployment. The Workload api doesn't specify how gang scheduling is applied to a specific "deployment" api (LWS, Deployment, StatefulSet etc.), it is more about how one sets the selectors. If one sets the selectors to define a gang as pods in a Deployment, then that Deployment's pods will be gang scheduled. For cases like LWS, which defines groups of pods as replicas, then the workload api also gives the ability to define "replicated gangs". So I don't believe there is inconsistency. 2) On minCount, this is specific to gang scheduling of pods (pods specifically, not "replicas", as in not LWS replicas, only pods within the gang) that should be scheduled in an all-or-nothing manner. Management of individual replicas, whether the replica is a group of pods (in LWS case) or individual pods (in Deployment case), is a separate matter from gang scheduling. 3) On minCount and the lack of guarantees for the leader, I indeed think this is a gap, but it should be possible to amend the api to take this case into account. Great catch! 4) On managing groups of replicas (for example at least x prefill and y decode), whether a replica is a pod or a group of pods, this is not looked at as a gang-scheduling (all-or-nothing) problem per se; k8s has an API called PodDisruptionBudget (PDB), admittedly the name is legacy and is focused on Pods, but there is an effort to change that to give it "Replica Disruption Budget" semantics so that we can apply the concept on application apis like LWS. However, as you mention in the second gap, I agree that we should revisit this and discuss if scheduling policies across replicas is a concept that we want to bring to the new Workload api, keep it in PDB or propose a third api. The current gang-scheduling capability in the workload api (which again is pod-centric) covers some of this for the single-node case only because for single-node a replica is a pod, not because it is intentionally trying to support it for single-node and not for multi-node.
